title: Talk to Right Specialists: Iterative Routing in Multi-agent Systems for Question Answering
abstract_text: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) agents are increasingly deployed to answer questions over local knowledge bases that cannot be centralized due to knowledgesovereignty constraints. This results in two recurring failures in production: users do not know which agent to consult, and complex questions require evidence distributed across multiple agents. To overcome these challenges, we propose RIRS, a training-free orchestration framework to enable a multi-agent system for question answering. In detail, RIRS summarizes each agent's local corpus in an embedding space, enabling a user-facing server to route queries only to the most relevant agents, reducing latency and avoiding noisy "broadcast-to-all" contexts. For complicated questions, the server can iteratively aggregate responses to derive intermediate results and refine the question to bridge the gap toward a comprehensive answer. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of RIRS, including its ability to precisely select agents and provide accurate responses to single-hop queries, and its use of an iterative strategy to achieve accurate, multistep resolutions for complex queries.

IntroductionRetrieval-augmented generation (RAG) improves the reliability of large language model (LLM) applications by grounding model outputs in retrieved external evidence (Wu et al., 2024c;Asai et al., 2023a;Lewis et al., 2020;Jiang et al., 2023;Izacard & Grave, 2020;Mallen et al., 2022;Kasai et al., 2024;Xiong et al., 2024;Weng, 2023;Roucher, 2024;Joshi et al., 2024). In practice, this capability is often deployed as a RAG agent backed by a private corpus. However, enterprise knowledge is rarely centralized: different business units, products, or teams often maintain separate RAG agents over disjoint corpora, such as internal documentation, contracts, incident reports, or partner data (Addison et al., 2024;Wu et al., 2024a;b). Centralizing these corpora into a single repository (Figure 1a) is typically infeasible due to governance constraints, access controls, and confidentiality requirements. Moreover, as we show in Section 3.2, centralization is not only desirable due to knowledge sovereignty constraints, but also hurts retrieval quality and downstream reasoning. This setting raises a fundamental systems question: how can a user-facing server answer questions when the relevant evidence is distributed across multiple specialized RAG agents and cannot be pooled into a single repository?A natural orchestration strategy is broadcast-to-all: as illustrated in Figure 1b, a user-facing server forwards each query to every RAG agent, aggregates their responses, and repeats this process until a final answer is produced. In this system, each agent retains its local, domain-specific knowledge base, ensuring that its knowledge sovereignty is well protected and that its data are not merged into a centralized repository. However, broadcast-to-all is inefficient in practice: (i) it wastes computation and communication because many agents are irrelevant to a given query, (ii) it increases end-to-end latency by waiting for slow agents and processing long concatenated responses, and (iii) it can degrade answer quality because excessively long and noisy context makes it easy for the model to overlook the right evidence (the "lost-in-the-middle" problem), as demonstrated in Section 3.3. These limitations motivate a distributed multi-agent system with a routing mechanism that selects only the most appropriate agents (treated as specialists) for each query, as illustrated in Figure 1c.Existing routing methods generally fall into two categories: description-based and learning-based.Description-based methods rely on manually written descriptions of agent capabilities, allowing an LLM to select the most suitable agent for a given query based on these descriptions (Patil et al., 2024;Lu et al., 2024a;b;Yuan et al., 2025;Wu et al., 2025;Zheng et al., 2026). In contrast, learningbased methods train a router on task-specific data to direct each user query to the most appropriate agent (Lu et al., 2023;Chen et al., 2024a;Ong et al., 2024;Yue et al., 2025;Mei et al., 2025;Wei et al., 2025;Wang et al., 2026). However, both strategies are difficult to apply in multi-RAG-agent settings. A textual description may not accurately capture the knowledge boundary of an agent whose corpus covers multiple subtopics. Learning-based methods are also problematic because the effective capability of a RAG agent is determined by its non-parametric local corpus, not only by parametric knowledge, and it is difficult to construct an effective dataset that fully covers that corpus. Therefore, a routing mechanism in a multi-RAG-agent system should accurately characterize an agent's knowledge capabilities without requiring raw data sharing or expensive training.In this work, we introduce RIRS, a practical orchestration framework that turns a collection of RAG agents into a single, coordinated problem-solving pipeline via Routing and Iterative Refining-Solving. Specifically, this framework consists of two modules, namely, knowledge summarization and query solving. In the knowledge summarization stage, each agent encodes its local corpus, partitions the resulting embeddings into coherent clusters, and uploads only cluster centroids to the server. These centroids provide a compact embedding-space summary of the agent's knowledge capabilities, while keeping raw knowledge local. In the query-solving stage, the server routes each query to the most relevant agents by matching the query embedding to the uploaded centroids. For complex queries, the server then iteratively evaluates partial responses, refines the unresolved question, and continues querying only the agents needed for the remaining subproblem. In this way, RIRS avoids broadcast-to-all, preserves knowledge sovereignty, and supports evidence composition across agents and across rounds.to enhance the quality and reliability of generated responses (Lewis et al., 2020;Chen et al., 2017;Guu et al., 2020;Karpukhin et al., 2020;Izacard & Grave, 2020;Borgeaud et al., 2022;Yu, 2022;Shi et al., 2023;Yan et al., 2024;Li et al., 2023b;Press et al., 2022;Chan et al., 2024;Su et al., 2024;Trivedi et al., 2022a;Ma et al., 2023;Shao et al., 2023;Zhang et al., 2025a), and there is a detailed description of how an RAG agent works in Section 3.1. Recent work has increasingly moved toward agentic RAG, where the model actively plans retrieval, refines queries, critiques intermediate results, and iterates between retrieval and reasoning to handle complex questions more effectively (Asai et al., 2023b;Jiang et al., 2023;Zhuang et al., 2024;Verma et al., 2024;Yang et al., 2024b;Singh et al., 2025;Li et al., 2025). These advances improve a single RAG pipeline, typically over a centralized knowledge source. In contrast, our work studies a distributed setting in which knowledge is partitioned across multiple RAG agents, so the main challenge is not only iterative reasoning, but also routing the query to the right agents and composing evidence across agents and rounds.Multi-agent Systems. Multi-agent systems leverage multiple specialized LLM-based agents to collaboratively solve complex tasks, and have attracted growing attention in recent years (Hong et al., 2023;Li et al., 2023a;Wu et al., 2023;Chen et al., 2023a;b;Zhao et al., 2023;Guo et al., 2024;Chen et al., 2024b;Li et al., 2024;Ye et al., 2025;Liu et al., 2026). In question answering, a growing number of studies improve answer quality through multi-agent collaboration, such as debate-or discussion-based frameworks in which multiple agents reason over a shared or common knowledge source to refine candidate answers (Zhang et al., 2025b;Iannelli et al., 2024;Du et al., 2024;Zhang et al., 2025a). These methods primarily emphasize better coordination and reasoning among agents once the knowledge source becomes accessible. Different from these works, our focus is not on having multiple agents reason over the same repository, but on identifying the most relevant agents when knowledge is inherently distributed across agents.
Preliminary and MotivationsThis section first reviews the pipelines of a RAG agent and a multi-RAG-agent system (Section 3.1).We then motivate multi-agent design by showing that multi-RAG-agent systems can consistently outperform single-agent baselines (Section 3.2), and by highlighting why an effective routing mechanism is crucial (Section 3.3).
Preliminary RAG Agent.An RAG agent is an advanced application that integrates retrieval mechanisms with LLMs to deliver accurate and contextually rich responses. Specifically, an RAG agent processes an input query through three steps: (i) Knowledge Retrieval: It extracts relevant knowledge pieces using both sparse and dense retrievers from external sources (Robertson et al., 2004;Izacard et al., 2021;Xu et al., 2023); (ii) Reranking: It ranks those retrieved pieces with a pretrained regression model to identify the likelihood of a knowledge piece helpful to the input query, thereby filtering out unhelpful or misleading information and allowing the generation model to focus on the most pertinent content;(iii) Response Generation: It combines the question and the pertinent external knowledge to produce an informed response with its backbone LLM. This process is also known as RankRAG (Yu et al., 2024). For multi-hop questions, it can adopt EfficientRAG (Zhuang et al., 2024) to iteratively refine the query and repeat retrieval and generation until the question is resolved.
Multi-RAG-Agent System.A multi-RAG-agent system consists of numerous RAG agents orchestrated under a central entity (i.e., server). When a user query comes, the system should repeatedly follow these three steps until the query is resolved: (i) the server selects a group of agents and forwards the query to them; (ii) the chosen RAG agent should give a response to the best of its local knowledge; (iii) the server aggregates the responses from the selected agents and simplifies the queries. While answering a given query, an RAG agent is supposed not to expose local raw knowledge, thereby preserving agent privacy and knowledge sovereignty. Such a system is also known as the federated RAG system in some recent works (Addison et al., 2024;Shi et al., 2025;Jung et al., 2025;Zhao, 2024).
Single-RAG-Agent System Does NOT WorkIn a single-RAG-agent system (Figure 1a), one agent collects and stores all documents in a single repository. Such centralization is often impractical in deployments due to knowledge-sovereignty concerns. Additionally, we analyze its performance limitation by comparing it with a practical multi- RAG-agent system. Table 1 compares three baselines that isolate retrieval and agent organization.
Chain-of-Thought (CoT) uses only the LLM's parametric knowledge.GoldRouter is an oracle upper bound for a multi-RAG-agent system that always routes each step to the relevant agents and aggregates their evidence.The results in the table confirm that RAG-based methods consistently outperform CoT, a method relying on a model's intrinsic memorization and reasoning capacities. Among all RAG-based baselines, the table demonstrates that GoldRouter consistently outperforms EfficientRAG, achieving up to a 5% improvement in GPT-evaluated accuracy. Furthermore, GoldRouter shows significant advantages over baseline methods within single-RAG-agent systems on multi-hop QA datasets (i.e., HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, MuSiQue). This performance gain underscores the inherent challenges of managing a large-scale knowledge repository: retrieving relevant information from large-scale, aggregated knowledge bases often includes irrelevant or distracting content, consequently limiting overall performance. Such extraneous content significantly complicates multi-hop reasoning, making it challenging to effectively simplify questions by discarding resolved portions of the query. In contrast, the multi-agent approach enables each agent to concentrate on a smaller, domain-specific set of documents, enhancing the relevance and precision of information retrieval. As a result, the multi-agent system can have a higher upper bound of the final performance. A naive way to avoid routing errors is allagent participation (Figure 1b): the server broadcasts the query to every agent and aggregates all responses. Table 2 shows that even on single-hop QA, this strategy is less accurate and much slower. For example, with Qwen-Plus, accuracy drops from 83.02 to 67.76 and latency rises from 12.97s to 72.91s; similar trends hold for LLaMA-3.1-8B, and the cost becomes prohibitive for multi-hop queries because broadcasting repeats across rounds. This gap is driven by irrelevant agent involvement: agents without useful evidence still consume computation, introduce distracting content, and force the server to wait for slow responses. The resulting long, noisy context makes evidence fusion harder and can reduce correctness. Therefore, a multi-RAG-agent system needs a routing mechanism that selects a small but sufficient subset of agents per round and supports knowledge fusion across rounds.
All-Agent Participation Does NOT Work
RIRSRIRS is designed for a practical multi-agent QA setting in which knowledge is distributed across specialized RAG agents, but users still expect a single accurate answer. In this setting, the main challenge is not only to find relevant agents, but also to combine their partial evidence into a coherent solution. A useful system therefore needs to do two things well: limit participation to agents that are likely to help, and continue reasoning when the answer must be assembled across multiple steps.To make this possible, RIRS decomposes the system into offline and online stages, as illustrated in Figure 2. At the offline stage (Figure 2a), each agent periodically summarizes the structure of its local knowledge in the embedding space and shares only a few lightweight representations with the server. At the online stage (Figure 2b), the server uses these summaries to route the query, judge the quality of returned responses, and iterate when necessary. Offline Agent-Side Preparation: Knowledge SummarizationAs shown in Figure 2a, each agent periodically summarizes its local knowledge base into a small set of centroids for routing. Concretely, an agent splits its local corpus into m chunks and encodes each chunk into an embedding vector e 1 , . . . , e m using a shared embedding model, where these embeddings are cached for later retrieval process. The agent then partitions these embeddings into n clusters and uploads only the resulting cluster centroids (along with an agent identifier) to the server. This design preserves knowledge sovereignty by keeping raw knowledge pieces local, while still allowing the server to estimate which RAG agents are relevant to a query in the embedding space.To make centroids reliable routing signals, clusters must be internally coherent. If a cluster mixes semantically unrelated pieces, its centroid degenerates into an "average topic" and becomes a weak relevance signal. We therefore formulate clustering as a max-min objective that encourages every cluster to be tight. Let {c 1 , . . . , c n } be a partition of {e 1 , . . . , e m } into n non-empty clusters, and let sim(•, •) denote cosine similarity. We maximize the worst-case within-cluster similarity:{c ⋆ k } n k=1 ∈ arg max {c k } n k=1 min k∈[n] min e a ,e b ∈c k a̸ =b sim(e a , e b ) s.t. {c k } n k=1 is a partition of {e 1 , . . . , e m }.(1)This objective prevents the optimization from sacrificing low-quality clusters because the least coherent cluster controls the objective value. As a result, each centroid is a faithful representative of a semantically consistent region of the agent's knowledge base.In practice, each agent optimizes Equation (1) through an approximate max-min similarity clustering algorithm (Algorithm 1) to obtain n disjoint clusters over its local embeddings. Starting from singleton clusters, the algorithm first normalizes the embeddings, computes pairwise cosine similarities, and iteratively merges the pair of current clusters with the largest bottleneck similarity until only n clusters remain. It then performs a local refinement stage that identifies the cluster with the smallest within-cluster bottleneck similarity, considers reassigning one endpoint of its worst-similarity pair to another cluster, and accepts the move only if it improves the objective in Equation (1). After obtaining the final partition, the agent computes one centroid for each cluster, i.e., the mean of its member embeddings, and uploads only these centroids to the server. In our experiments, we set n = ⌊ √ m⌋, where m is the number of local knowledge chunks. Full algorithmic details are provided in Appendix A.1, with pseudocode in Algorithm 1.

Online Query Solving via Routing and Iterative Refining-SolvingAs shown in Figure 2b, the uploaded centroids provide the server with an embedding-space approximation of each agent's knowledge capability: each centroid represents a coherent region where the agent is likely to contain supporting evidence. Given a query, the server embeds it and compares the query embedding with the uploaded centroids to identify the most appropriate agents. After receiving responses from the selected agents, the server evaluates whether those responses adequately address the query. If the query is not fully resolved, the server rewrites it to focus on the remaining unresolved aspects and then repeats the routing and response-evaluation process until a final answer is produced or no further progress can be made.

The server then applies Response Evaluator to label each response as addressed vs. not addressed and curates the round output (e.g., selecting or combining addressed responses). We denote this single-round procedure as RTANS(q), which includes: (i) TopK centroid-based agent selection, (ii) agent response generation with local evidence, (iii) server-side response evaluation, and (iv) response curation. For single-hop queries, a single RTANS call is typically sufficient.Iterative refining-solving for multi-hop queries. For multi-hop queries, the required evidence may be distributed across agents and across reasoning steps, so a single RTANS(q) call can be insufficient. RIRS repeats RTANS in an iterative loop. At iteration t, the server calls RTANS(q t ) and uses the Response Evaluator to label responses as fully addressed, partially addressed, or not addressed. If any response is fully addressed, the Response Summarizer consolidates the evidence-backed responses into the final answer and terminates. If only partially addressed responses exist, the server aggregates partial progress, invokes the Question Simplifier to produce a refined query q t+1 targeting unresolved aspects, and then proceeds to the next iteration. If all responses are not addressed, the server stops and reports that the query is unanswerable within the system scope. Full step-by-step procedures and server-module prompts are provided in Appendix A.Practical properties. RIRS has three practical advantages. First, centroid-based routing activates only a small set of relevant agents for each query, reducing fan-out, token usage, and interference from irrelevant responses. Second, for complex questions, the iterative refining-solving loop turns partial progress into targeted follow-up queries, enabling evidence composition across agents and across rounds. Third, RIRS cleanly separates offline knowledge summarization from online query solving: agents can update local knowledge, refresh their centroids, and synchronize them with the server, while the server maintains only a lightweight routing index. This separation simplifies new agent onboarding, supports continuous knowledge updates, and avoids centralizing raw corpora or retraining a router. 5 Experiments
Experimental SetupDue to space limits, this section summarizes the experimental setup needed to interpret our quantitative results. Full implementation details and baseline specifications are provided in Appendix B.
Datasets.Our experiments cover both single-hop and multi-hop open-ended QA tasks within a unified evaluation framework. We employ the Natural Questions (NQ) dataset (Kwiatkowski et al., 2019) for single-hop QA to emphasize the effectiveness of the routing mechanism. For evaluating the performance on answering complex questions, we assess performance on four multi-hop QA benchmarks: HotpotQA (Yang et al., 2018), 2WikiMultiQA (Ho et al., 2020), MusiQue (Trivedi et al., 2022b), and Multi-Hop RAG (MHR) Benchmark (Tang & Yang, 2024). Except for MHR, all questions in these datasets are answerable using knowledge from Wikipedia.
Models.We use text-embedding-v2 (Zhang et al., 2024) to compute dense representations for retrieval. Agents are powered by two LLM backends: llama-3.1-8b-instruct (Touvron et al., 2023a;b;Dubey et al., 2024) and qwen-plus-2024-12-20 (Yang et al., 2024a). All methods are evaluated in an off-the-shelf setting without fine-tuning.
Multi-RAG-Agent Systems.Throughout the experiments, we construct two multi-RAG-agent systems tailored to different datasets.• WikiAgents for NQ, HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiQA and MusiQue: WikiAgents group is built upon a corpus of over 121K Wikipedia pages, dumped as of November 1, 2023, and made publicly available via the HuggingFace dataset. The system comprises exactly 64 RAG agents. This specific number is derived from the inherent limitation of the ORES legacy service, which can only classify a Wikipedia page into 64 predefined categories (Johnson et al., 2021). Consequently, each RAG agent is designated to handle one of these 64 categories, ensuring that the categorization of pages is consistent and aligned with the predefined taxonomy established by the ORES service. However, these agents cannot cover all required documents, and once the question cannot be answered, a knowledgeable agent will be called to answer the question because the existing LLMs have been pretrained with the Wikipedia corpus.• NewsAgents for MHR: NewsAgents group is constructed on a corpus of 609 news articles from 49 distinct news media and spanning six domains (Tang & Yang, 2024). To analyze the effects of source and domain characteristics, we further split NewsAgent into two variants: NewsAgent-Source and NewsAgent-Domain, corresponding to partitions based on news media and domain categories, respectively. Each agent uses LLaMAIndex to split news articles into 256-token chunks, with 20 overlapping tokens between consecutive chunks.Baselines. We compare RIRS with two representative multi-agent routing baselines. Chameleon (Lu et al., 2024a) is a description-based router that maintains a textual description for each agent and prompts an LLM to select the most relevant agents for a given query. RouterDC (Chen et al., 2024a) is a learning-based router that constructs agent representations from single-hop answerable questions and routes by embedding similarity while keeping the embedding model fixed. Both methods operate in the same multi-RAG-agent setting as RIRS and serve as alternative routing strategies. Further implementation details are provided in Appendix B.3.Evaluation Metrics. We report three metrics. Lexical Match (LM) measures the percentage of questions whose ground-truth answer string appears in the generated response. GPT Evaluation (Acc.) uses gpt-4o-2024-08-06 (Achiam et al., 2023) to judge correctness by comparing model outputs against ground-truth answers while allowing paraphrases. Time measures wall-clock latency from receiving the question to producing a seemingly valid response; this metric can be noisy due to network/API variance and runtime contention. 
Ablation StudiesChoice of TopK. Table 3 shows that selecting more clusters increases both agent-level and document-level answerable rates, which generally improves end-to-end LM/Acc. at the cost of invoking more agents and viewing more documents. A key observation is that increasing TopK from 1 to 5 yields a substantial gain, while further increasing it from 5 to 10 brings only marginal improvement, suggesting diminishing returns beyond moderate agent coverage. Notably, the final accuracy can exceed the answerable rate because the system falls back to a CoT-only response when the selected agents are judged unable to answer; in such cases, the LLM may still answer correctly using parametric knowledge. Finally, document-level answerable rates are consistently lower than agent-level rates, indicating that even when the right agent is selected, retrieval within its local index may still miss the most relevant evidence.
Analysis with Wikipedia-related QATable 4 compares the proposed RIRS with representative multi-agent routing baselines on four Wikipedia-based QA benchmarks under the WikiAgents corpus. We summarize the most salient findings below.Comparison with GoldRouter. As an error-free routing mechanism, GoldRouter serves as the upper bound in a multi-agent system, achieving the highest scores in LM, F1, and Accuracy, as well as the lowest values in rounds and response time. In contrast, all other methods (Chameleon, RouterDC, and RIRS) experience varying degrees of performance degradation. i.e., more query rounds but with lower accuracy. The degradation is owed to routing errors, highlighting the importance of designing an effective routing mechanism and underscoring the inherent challenge of dynamically estimating each agent's expertise on-the-fly.Comparison with other routing methods. From Table 4, the accuracy ranking among the three routing methods consistently follows: RIRS > Chameleon > RouterDC, under the same dataset and backbone LLM. The advantage of RIRS is especially clear on harder multi-hop benchmarks and with the weaker backbone (LLaMA-3.1-8B), where RIRS improves accuracy by up to 8% over Chameleon and 15% over RouterDC. These results suggest that RIRS more reliably identifies agent knowledge boundaries. Concretely, RIRS builds cluster-level representations to characterize each agent's knowledge capacity, enabling more accurate routing. By contrast, RouterDC approximates agent expertise via a fixed cache of historically answerable questions, and Chameleon relies on static textual descriptions; both signals can be incomplete and lead to misrouting. Notably, while RIRS may use slightly more rounds than Chameleon, it often runs faster overall because it avoids additional LLM calls during agent selection.Comparison with various LLMs. Using a stronger backbone (Qwen-Plus) consistently improves all methods over LLaMA-3.1-8B, as expected. Moreover, the mixed setting, which uses a stronger server-side controller (Qwen-Plus) with lightweight agent models, recovers much of the performance of Qwen-Plus while keeping agent-side costs low. Together with the response-evaluator results in Table 7, this suggests that a strong evaluator/controller is critical for reducing error propagation when intermediate agent responses are noisy. This design makes RIRS practical for deployment: Lightweight models can run at the RAG agents, allowing the underlying knowledge bases to remain local and generating evidence-backed responses even in resource-constrained settings. Meanwhile, the user-facing server is equipped with a stronger model to ensure the final response is precise.

Compared with Chameleon, the gap is particularly pronounced under NewsAgent-Source, where outletlevel descriptions are often too coarse because a single outlet can cover many unrelated topics. In the more structured NewsAgent-Domain setting, Chameleon becomes stronger but still lags behind RIRS. Discussion of Different Numbers of RAG Agents. From Table 5 and Figure 3, we observe a tradeoff between granularity and routing reliability. Using more agents provides finer-grained coverage and typically reduces the number of rounds needed to locate relevant evidence. However, a larger agent pool also increases routing uncertainty and can hurt accuracy. Compared with GoldRouter, performance degradation is more pronounced under NewsAgent-Source than under NewsAgent-Domain. We attribute this gap to suboptimal agent formation in NewsAgent-Source: partitioning by news outlets yields agents with diverse, weakly structured topic coverage, which makes it harder to route queries to the right agents. Besides, the much larger number of agents in NewsAgent-Source further amplifies routing uncertainty.A closer comparison between the single-RAG-agent system and NewsAgent-Domain reveals the existence of an optimal number of agents for a given knowledge base. Using too few agents can lead to overly broad domain coverage, which reintroduces the challenge of retrieving irrelevant information. In contrast, the domain-based configuration results in more efficient and accurate resolution of complex, multi-hop questions.
ConclusionWe study how to reliably answer user queries when knowledge is distributed across multiple business units and cannot be centralized due to privacy, compliance, or ownership constraints. To this end, we propose RIRS, an iterative routing framework that coordinates multiple RAG agents while preserving knowledge sovereignty. RIRS decouples offline knowledge summarization from online query solving: each agent summarizes its local corpus into centroid-based representations in the embedding space and maintains these summaries independently, while a user-facing server performs iterative refiningsolving and fuses evidence across agents and rounds. Experiments show that RIRS consistently outperforms strong multi-agent baselines, and its architecture supports practical deployment: agents can run lightweight models for grounded generation with local corpora, while the server uses a stronger model to synthesize reliable responses.
Ethics StatementThis work studies a realistic multi-agent question-answering setting in which knowledge is distributed across RAG agents and cannot be centralized. The proposed framework reduces unnecessary data exposure by sharing embedding-space summaries for routing. However, this design does not address two potential risks. In an agent-in-the-wild setting, malicious agents may return incomplete, misleading, or low-quality responses, and routing or evaluation errors may propagate across iterations, especially for complex multi-hop questions. To reduce this risk, RIRS requires evidence-backed responses, filters returned outputs through a server-side evaluator, and allows the system to stop or declare a query unanswerable when adequate support is unavailable. A second concern is privacy leakage: Similar to federated learning, the proposed RIRS offers a fundamental privacy protection because centroid summaries are more restrictive than sharing raw documents. However, it still reveals partial information about local knowledge, especially under repeated probing or after updates to an agent's corpus. An important direction for future work is to study how additional privacy-preserving mechanisms, such as Gaussian or Laplace perturbation, affect routing accuracy, and to develop stronger privacy-preserving summarization and access-control mechanisms that preserve comparable performance.
Reproducibility StatementWe make reproducibility a priority in both the algorithmic design and the experimental setup. A.1 Optimization of Equation (1): Approximate Max-Min Similarity ClusteringEquation ( 1) seeks a partition of the local embeddings into n non-empty clusters that maximizes the smallest within-cluster cosine similarity. Exact optimization over all partitions is combinatorial. We therefore adopt a two-stage greedy approximation, summarized in Algorithm 1. The first stage is motivated by classic work on hierarchical clustering and greedy complete-linkage agglomeration (Everitt et al., 2011;Murtagh & Contreras, 2012;Sharma et al., 2019). The second stage adds an R-round local refinement to further improve the max-min objective.Let êi = e i /∥e i ∥ denote the normalized embedding of knowledge piece i, and let S ij = ê⊤ i êj be the cosine similarity between normalized embeddings. For any non-empty cluster C, define its bottleneck similarity by b(C) := +∞, |C| ≤ 1,min i,j∈C, i<j S ij , |C| ≥ 2.For a partition C = {C 1 , . . . , C n }, define the partition bottleneck objective B(C) := min k∈[n] b(C k ).Then Equation ( 1) is equivalent to maximizing B(C) over all partitions into n non-empty clusters.Stage I: Cached complete-link clustering. We initialize each embedding as a singleton cluster. For two current clusters A and B, define their merge score by g(A, B) := min i∈A, j∈B S ij .At each step, Stage I merges the pair of active clusters with the largest value of g(A, B). This rule is the complete-link analogue of greedy agglomeration: it favors merges whose worst cross-cluster pair is as strong as possible, and thus delays deterioration of the smallest within-cluster similarity. To make this stage efficient, we cache inter-cluster bottleneck scores and maintain candidate merges in a max-heap. After a merge M = A ∪ B, the score between M and any other active cluster C is updated by g(M, C) = min{g(A, C), g(B, C)}, which is the standard complete-link recurrence. The procedure is easiest to describe under a mild generic-position assumption that distinct embedding pairs have distinct cosine similarities. Under this assumption, the worst cluster and the worst pair at each round are uniquely defined. A.2 Effectiveness of Knowledge SummarizationThis subsection provides additional justification for centroid-based routing in RIRS. In the offline stage (Section 4.1), each RAG agent partitions its local knowledge-piece embeddings into disjoint clusters and uploads only the corresponding centroids to the server. At inference time, the server routes a user query by retrieving the most similar centroids and selecting the associated agents/clusters.The key intuition is that if a cluster is semantically coherent, then its centroid remains a reliable proxy for locating that cluster (and thus the responsible RAG agent) using cosine similarity.We formalize this intuition in a similarity-bounded (threshold-based) clustering setting and show that centroid-based search is bounded: a query cannot be simultaneously very close to a relevant knowledge piece and arbitrarily far from the centroid of the piece's cluster. This bound clarifies when centroid routing is reliable and how clustering quality (coherence) impacts routing robustness.

Theorems A.1 and A.2 imply that centroid-based routing is bounded under the scoherence assumption: if a query is close to a relevant knowledge piece (large k) and clusters are coherent (large s), then the query cannot be arbitrarily far from the corresponding centroid. Therefore, the following failure mode cannot occur in an unbounded way: "a highly specific user query may be very close to the most relevant single knowledge piece but relatively far from the centroid vector of the entire cluster to which the knowledge piece belongs." In practice, centroids can still be less similar than the best individual knowledge piece (because they average multiple pieces), but the gap is bounded by the expression in Theorem A.2.Practical design choices: TopK selection and square-root clusters. While the threshold-based setup enables analysis, production deployment requires controllable routing cost and stable latency. In RIRS, we therefore adopt two practical choices.First, we select candidate clusters (and thus RAG agents) by TopK, as described in Section 4.2. A similarity-threshold rule (select all centroids with similarity greater than a designated threshold) is difficult to control: broad queries can match many centroids, leading to unpredictable fan-out and unstable latency/cost. Although Theorem A.2 relates cluster coherence to query-centroid similarity, any analytically "safe" threshold can be overly permissive in realistic regimes, still admitting many weakly related clusters. In contrast, TopK is a direct, monotone cost knob and is commonly used to achieve controllable latency and budget constraints.Second, as mentioned in Section 4.1, we set the number of clusters per agent to n = ⌊ √ m⌋. This heuristic is inspired by the success of inverted file indexing in database practice: it provides a predictable, sublinear growth of the number of centroids, limiting server-side storage and similaritysearch cost. Intuitively, agents with more knowledge pieces may have more overlapping or redundant content and thus can be represented with more clusters, while agents with fewer knowledge pieces are often more specialized and do not require fine-grained partitioning. This design choice is also supported empirically: Table 6 shows that square-root clustering achieves comparable accuracy to threshold-based clustering while requiring substantially fewer clusters per agent, reducing server-side index/storage overhead.A similarity threshold can also be used to determine the number of clusters, but it is difficult to calibrate: a high threshold may produce many small clusters, inflating the number of uploaded centroids and thus the server's index size. Moreover, under global TopK selection, an excessive number of clusters per agent can reduce cross-agent coverage: multiple centroids from the same agent may occupy the TopK list, decreasing the number of unique selected agents and harming performance on cross-domain queries. For these reasons, we adopt the square-root heuristic and TopK selection as a production-friendly default.
A.3 Server ModulesRIRS coordinates multiple RAG agents using a central server. Beyond routing, the server relies on several server modules to (i) filter unreliable or irrelevant responses, (ii) consolidate evidence-backed content, and (iii) refine queries when multi-hop reasoning is required. These server modules do not maintain private knowledge bases; they operate only on the user query, the routed RAG agent responses, and the quoted evidence returned by those RAG agents. Prompt templates are provided in Figures 9 to 11.Response Evaluator (Prompt in Figure 9). The Response Evaluator is the first checkpoint after collecting responses from selected RAG agents. Since the server lacks domain-specific knowledge, the evaluator uses a common-sense and logic-based assessment with three criteria: (i) Relevance: whether the response helps answer the query (even if incomplete); (ii) Evidence-based support: whether key claims are supported by explicitly quoted evidence; and (iii) Logical coherence: whether the response is consistent and free of contradictions. For single-hop settings, the evaluator labels each response as addressed or not addressed. For multi-hop settings, it further distinguishes fully addressed from partially addressed among the addressed responses. This filtering is critical because irrelevant RAG agents may still produce plausible but misleading responses; propagating such responses can degrade summarization and cause error accumulation across rounds.Response Summarizer (Prompt in Figure 10). The Response Summarizer consolidates evaluatorapproved responses into either a final answer or an intermediate solution. When at least one response is labeled fully addressed, the summarizer produces the final answer by integrating evidence-backed content from one or more fully addressed responses. When no response is fully addressed but some are partially addressed, the summarizer first synthesizes a unified intermediate solution from the valid partial evidence and then re-evaluates whether the unified solution fully resolves the query. If it is deemed fully addressed, the summarizer outputs the final answer; otherwise, it outputs the intermediate solution for query refinement. This design benefits from evaluator filtering, since summarization is more reliable when the input is shorter and contains fewer irrelevant responses.Question Simplifier (Prompt in Figure 11). When the current query is not fully resolved, the Question Simplifier refines it for the next round. Given the original query and the current intermediate solution, it: (i) identifies which components of the query have already been addressed (with evidence), (ii) enumerates unresolved aspects that remain necessary for correctness, and (iii) generates a refined query that removes resolved parts and focuses on unresolved aspects. This on-the-fly refinement converts partial progress into a targeted next query, enabling iterative multi-hop progress without requiring a rigid precomputed question decomposition plan.

A.5 Discussion: Unhandleable QueriesEven with centroid-based routing and iterative refining-solving, some queries remain unanswerable within the system scope or operational constraints. This can occur for several reasons: (i) the query falls outside the knowledge coverage of all RAG agents; (ii) the query is ambiguous, underspecified, or noisy (e.g., due to typos), hindering routing and retrieval; (iii) the relevant domain evolves rapidly, and agents' local knowledge bases become stale; or (iv) retrieval/evaluation fails under practical constraints (timeouts, round limits), preventing evidence-backed progress.Practical handling. In practice, systems typically adopt one of two policies. First, they may return an explicit unanswerable response to the user and request rephrasing or additional context. Second, they may escalate the query to a human expert, especially in high-stakes settings, optionally forwarding the system's intermediate progress and collected evidence to reduce human effort.What we adopt in this work. Our handling differs across settings. In WikiAgents, a true humanexpert escalation is operationally expensive. We therefore approximate this pathway by invoking a knowledgeable agent when RIRS fails to obtain any addressed responses (or reaches the round limit). For multi-hop queries, the knowledgeable agent is given a simplified query produced by the Question Simplifier when available, since reducing the number of reasoning steps is often beneficial (Zhuang et al., 2024). In NewsAgent, each input query includes a label indicating whether it is solvable. For queries labeled unsolvable (or when no evidence-backed, addressed responses are obtained), we return an explicit unanswerable response to the user rather than attempting a fallback that could increase hallucination risk in time-sensitive domains.
B Implementations and Baselines
B.1 System Implementation DetailsOur implementation builds upon the open-source AgentScope project (Gao et al., 2024). Each agent's knowledge base is processed by LLaMAIndex (Liu, 2022) and stored in ElasticSearch. We use ElasticSearch mixed retrieval (BM25 + dense vectors) for retrieval. For each selected agent, we retrieve 20 candidate chunks and retain the best five chunks for answer generation. Unless otherwise specified, no more than five agents are selected per routing iteration.The system is deployed in a pseudo-distributed environment using multi-threading to improve throughput. For model serving, we call Qwen-Plus via API (Yang et al., 2024a;Bai et al., 2023) and deploy LLaMA-3.1-8B locally using vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023) on four Nvidia A100 GPUs.
B.2 Agent Construction and CorporaWikiAgents. WikiAgents is built over 121K Wikipedia pages (snapshot date: Nov. 1, 2023) and contains exactly 64 agents. This number follows the limitation of the ORES legacy service, which assigns Wikipedia pages into 64 predefined categories (Johnson et al., 2021); we map each category to one agent so that agent specialization aligns with the ORES taxonomy. Because this taxonomy may not cover all documents required by downstream questions, when retrieved evidence is insufficient, the LLM may still respond based on its parametric knowledge. We account for this behavior in evaluation by reporting both lexical match and LLM-judged accuracy (Section 5.1).NewsAgents. NewsAgents is constructed from 609 news articles from 49 media outlets across six domains (Tang & Yang, 2024). We consider two partitions: NewsAgent-Source (agents grouped by outlet) and NewsAgent-Domain (agents grouped by domain). Each agent uses LLaMAIndex to split articles into 256-token chunks with 20-token overlap between consecutive chunks.
B.3 BaselinesWe reproduce baselines within our multi-agent evaluation framework. All methods are evaluated in an off-the-shelf setting: we do not train any models, and instead rely on LLM capabilities.Single-agent Scenarios. In the single-agent setting, the knowledge contained within all RAG agents is merged into a single RAG system. This provides a conventional RAG baseline that can retrieve from the entire corpus. Although it does not fully match the multi-agent routing scenario, it illustrates challenges of large-scale retrieval (e.g., longer retrieval latency and increased distractors). If retrieval were perfectly clean, the single-agent setup could be viewed as an approximate upper bound for multi-agent accuracy when judged against ground truth; in practice, however, pooling all documents increases the chance of retrieving distractors, especially for multi-hop queries.• EfficientRAG (Zhuang et al., 2024): This approach iteratively simplifies/decomposes the query, retrieving evidence at each step until the question becomes answerable. The simplification process is performed by the LLM by removing resolved parts of the query; if further progress is not possible, a knowledgeable agent produces the final answer. Our implementation follows EfficientRAG (Zhuang et al., 2024) and is conceptually related to Self-ASK (Press et al., 2022), SelfRAG (Asai et al., 2023b), and IM-RAG (Yang et al., 2024b).Multi-agent Scenarios. In the multi-agent setting, we keep the same agent backends and retrieval modules as RIRS, and only replace the routing mechanism.• Chameleon (Lu et al., 2024a): A description-based router that prompts an LLM with agent descriptions and selects the agents most relevant to the current query. For WikiAgents, each description is derived from the corresponding ORES topic category. For NewsAgents, descriptions are derived from either the news outlet or the domain, depending on the partition.• RouterDC (Chen et al., 2024a): A learning-based router that represents each candidate agent with a learned routing vector and selects agents by embedding similarity at inference time. To instantiate this baseline in our setting, we collect 100 single-hop answerable questions for each WikiAgent and use them to fit agent representations while keeping the embedding backbone fixed. We do not report RouterDC on MHR because that benchmark does not provide enough agent-specific supervision to train these representations reliably.    Performance when Excluding Knowledgeable Agents.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.text: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) improves the reliability of large language model (LLM) applications by grounding model outputs in retrieved external evidence (Wu et al., 2024c;Asai et al., 2023a;Lewis et al., 2020;Jiang et al., 2023;Izacard & Grave, 2020;Mallen et al., 2022;Kasai et al., 2024;Xiong et al., 2024;Weng, 2023;Roucher, 2024;Joshi et al., 2024). In practice, this capability is often deployed as a RAG agent backed by a private corpus. However, enterprise knowledge is rarely centralized: different business units, products, or teams often maintain separate RAG agents over disjoint corpora, such as internal documentation, contracts, incident reports, or partner data (Addison et al., 2024;Wu et al., 2024a;b). Centralizing these corpora into a single repository (Figure 1a) is typically infeasible due to governance constraints, access controls, and confidentiality requirements. Moreover, as we show in Section 3.2, centralization is not only desirable due to knowledge sovereignty constraints, but also hurts retrieval quality and downstream reasoning. This setting raises a fundamental systems question: how can a user-facing server answer questions when the relevant evidence is distributed across multiple specialized RAG agents and cannot be pooled into a single repository?A natural orchestration strategy is broadcast-to-all: as illustrated in Figure 1b, a user-facing server forwards each query to every RAG agent, aggregates their responses, and repeats this process until a final answer is produced. In this system, each agent retains its local, domain-specific knowledge base, ensuring that its knowledge sovereignty is well protected and that its data are not merged into a centralized repository. However, broadcast-to-all is inefficient in practice: (i) it wastes computation and communication because many agents are irrelevant to a given query, (ii) it increases end-to-end latency by waiting for slow agents and processing long concatenated responses, and (iii) it can degrade answer quality because excessively long and noisy context makes it easy for the model to overlook the right evidence (the "lost-in-the-middle" problem), as demonstrated in Section 3.3. These limitations motivate a distributed multi-agent system with a routing mechanism that selects only the most appropriate agents (treated as specialists) for each query, as illustrated in Figure 1c.Existing routing methods generally fall into two categories: description-based and learning-based.Description-based methods rely on manually written descriptions of agent capabilities, allowing an LLM to select the most suitable agent for a given query based on these descriptions (Patil et al., 2024;Lu et al., 2024a;b;Yuan et al., 2025;Wu et al., 2025;Zheng et al., 2026). In contrast, learningbased methods train a router on task-specific data to direct each user query to the most appropriate agent (Lu et al., 2023;Chen et al., 2024a;Ong et al., 2024;Yue et al., 2025;Mei et al., 2025;Wei et al., 2025;Wang et al., 2026). However, both strategies are difficult to apply in multi-RAG-agent settings. A textual description may not accurately capture the knowledge boundary of an agent whose corpus covers multiple subtopics. Learning-based methods are also problematic because the effective capability of a RAG agent is determined by its non-parametric local corpus, not only by parametric knowledge, and it is difficult to construct an effective dataset that fully covers that corpus. Therefore, a routing mechanism in a multi-RAG-agent system should accurately characterize an agent's knowledge capabilities without requiring raw data sharing or expensive training.In this work, we introduce RIRS, a practical orchestration framework that turns a collection of RAG agents into a single, coordinated problem-solving pipeline via Routing and Iterative Refining-Solving. Specifically, this framework consists of two modules, namely, knowledge summarization and query solving. In the knowledge summarization stage, each agent encodes its local corpus, partitions the resulting embeddings into coherent clusters, and uploads only cluster centroids to the server. These centroids provide a compact embedding-space summary of the agent's knowledge capabilities, while keeping raw knowledge local. In the query-solving stage, the server routes each query to the most relevant agents by matching the query embedding to the uploaded centroids. For complex queries, the server then iteratively evaluates partial responses, refines the unresolved question, and continues querying only the agents needed for the remaining subproblem. In this way, RIRS avoids broadcast-to-all, preserves knowledge sovereignty, and supports evidence composition across agents and across rounds.to enhance the quality and reliability of generated responses (Lewis et al., 2020;Chen et al., 2017;Guu et al., 2020;Karpukhin et al., 2020;Izacard & Grave, 2020;Borgeaud et al., 2022;Yu, 2022;Shi et al., 2023;Yan et al., 2024;Li et al., 2023b;Press et al., 2022;Chan et al., 2024;Su et al., 2024;Trivedi et al., 2022a;Ma et al., 2023;Shao et al., 2023;Zhang et al., 2025a), and there is a detailed description of how an RAG agent works in Section 3.1. Recent work has increasingly moved toward agentic RAG, where the model actively plans retrieval, refines queries, critiques intermediate results, and iterates between retrieval and reasoning to handle complex questions more effectively (Asai et al., 2023b;Jiang et al., 2023;Zhuang et al., 2024;Verma et al., 2024;Yang et al., 2024b;Singh et al., 2025;Li et al., 2025). These advances improve a single RAG pipeline, typically over a centralized knowledge source. In contrast, our work studies a distributed setting in which knowledge is partitioned across multiple RAG agents, so the main challenge is not only iterative reasoning, but also routing the query to the right agents and composing evidence across agents and rounds.Multi-agent Systems. Multi-agent systems leverage multiple specialized LLM-based agents to collaboratively solve complex tasks, and have attracted growing attention in recent years (Hong et al., 2023;Li et al., 2023a;Wu et al., 2023;Chen et al., 2023a;b;Zhao et al., 2023;Guo et al., 2024;Chen et al., 2024b;Li et al., 2024;Ye et al., 2025;Liu et al., 2026). In question answering, a growing number of studies improve answer quality through multi-agent collaboration, such as debate-or discussion-based frameworks in which multiple agents reason over a shared or common knowledge source to refine candidate answers (Zhang et al., 2025b;Iannelli et al., 2024;Du et al., 2024;Zhang et al., 2025a). These methods primarily emphasize better coordination and reasoning among agents once the knowledge source becomes accessible. Different from these works, our focus is not on having multiple agents reason over the same repository, but on identifying the most relevant agents when knowledge is inherently distributed across agents.

sections.title: Preliminary and Motivations
sections.text: This section first reviews the pipelines of a RAG agent and a multi-RAG-agent system (Section 3.1).We then motivate multi-agent design by showing that multi-RAG-agent systems can consistently outperform single-agent baselines (Section 3.2), and by highlighting why an effective routing mechanism is crucial (Section 3.3).

sections.title: Preliminary RAG Agent.
sections.text: An RAG agent is an advanced application that integrates retrieval mechanisms with LLMs to deliver accurate and contextually rich responses. Specifically, an RAG agent processes an input query through three steps: (i) Knowledge Retrieval: It extracts relevant knowledge pieces using both sparse and dense retrievers from external sources (Robertson et al., 2004;Izacard et al., 2021;Xu et al., 2023); (ii) Reranking: It ranks those retrieved pieces with a pretrained regression model to identify the likelihood of a knowledge piece helpful to the input query, thereby filtering out unhelpful or misleading information and allowing the generation model to focus on the most pertinent content;(iii) Response Generation: It combines the question and the pertinent external knowledge to produce an informed response with its backbone LLM. This process is also known as RankRAG (Yu et al., 2024). For multi-hop questions, it can adopt EfficientRAG (Zhuang et al., 2024) to iteratively refine the query and repeat retrieval and generation until the question is resolved.

sections.title: Multi-RAG-Agent System.
sections.text: A multi-RAG-agent system consists of numerous RAG agents orchestrated under a central entity (i.e., server). When a user query comes, the system should repeatedly follow these three steps until the query is resolved: (i) the server selects a group of agents and forwards the query to them; (ii) the chosen RAG agent should give a response to the best of its local knowledge; (iii) the server aggregates the responses from the selected agents and simplifies the queries. While answering a given query, an RAG agent is supposed not to expose local raw knowledge, thereby preserving agent privacy and knowledge sovereignty. Such a system is also known as the federated RAG system in some recent works (Addison et al., 2024;Shi et al., 2025;Jung et al., 2025;Zhao, 2024).

sections.title: Single-RAG-Agent System Does NOT Work
sections.text: In a single-RAG-agent system (Figure 1a), one agent collects and stores all documents in a single repository. Such centralization is often impractical in deployments due to knowledge-sovereignty concerns. Additionally, we analyze its performance limitation by comparing it with a practical multi- RAG-agent system. Table 1 compares three baselines that isolate retrieval and agent organization.

sections.title: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) uses only the LLM's parametric knowledge.
sections.text: GoldRouter is an oracle upper bound for a multi-RAG-agent system that always routes each step to the relevant agents and aggregates their evidence.The results in the table confirm that RAG-based methods consistently outperform CoT, a method relying on a model's intrinsic memorization and reasoning capacities. Among all RAG-based baselines, the table demonstrates that GoldRouter consistently outperforms EfficientRAG, achieving up to a 5% improvement in GPT-evaluated accuracy. Furthermore, GoldRouter shows significant advantages over baseline methods within single-RAG-agent systems on multi-hop QA datasets (i.e., HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, MuSiQue). This performance gain underscores the inherent challenges of managing a large-scale knowledge repository: retrieving relevant information from large-scale, aggregated knowledge bases often includes irrelevant or distracting content, consequently limiting overall performance. Such extraneous content significantly complicates multi-hop reasoning, making it challenging to effectively simplify questions by discarding resolved portions of the query. In contrast, the multi-agent approach enables each agent to concentrate on a smaller, domain-specific set of documents, enhancing the relevance and precision of information retrieval. As a result, the multi-agent system can have a higher upper bound of the final performance. A naive way to avoid routing errors is allagent participation (Figure 1b): the server broadcasts the query to every agent and aggregates all responses. Table 2 shows that even on single-hop QA, this strategy is less accurate and much slower. For example, with Qwen-Plus, accuracy drops from 83.02 to 67.76 and latency rises from 12.97s to 72.91s; similar trends hold for LLaMA-3.1-8B, and the cost becomes prohibitive for multi-hop queries because broadcasting repeats across rounds. This gap is driven by irrelevant agent involvement: agents without useful evidence still consume computation, introduce distracting content, and force the server to wait for slow responses. The resulting long, noisy context makes evidence fusion harder and can reduce correctness. Therefore, a multi-RAG-agent system needs a routing mechanism that selects a small but sufficient subset of agents per round and supports knowledge fusion across rounds.

sections.title: RIRS
sections.text: RIRS is designed for a practical multi-agent QA setting in which knowledge is distributed across specialized RAG agents, but users still expect a single accurate answer. In this setting, the main challenge is not only to find relevant agents, but also to combine their partial evidence into a coherent solution. A useful system therefore needs to do two things well: limit participation to agents that are likely to help, and continue reasoning when the answer must be assembled across multiple steps.To make this possible, RIRS decomposes the system into offline and online stages, as illustrated in Figure 2. At the offline stage (Figure 2a), each agent periodically summarizes the structure of its local knowledge in the embedding space and shares only a few lightweight representations with the server. At the online stage (Figure 2b), the server uses these summaries to route the query, judge the quality of returned responses, and iterate when necessary. sections.title: Offline Agent-Side Preparation: Knowledge Summarization
sections.text: As shown in Figure 2a, each agent periodically summarizes its local knowledge base into a small set of centroids for routing. Concretely, an agent splits its local corpus into m chunks and encodes each chunk into an embedding vector e 1 , . . . , e m using a shared embedding model, where these embeddings are cached for later retrieval process. The agent then partitions these embeddings into n clusters and uploads only the resulting cluster centroids (along with an agent identifier) to the server. This design preserves knowledge sovereignty by keeping raw knowledge pieces local, while still allowing the server to estimate which RAG agents are relevant to a query in the embedding space.To make centroids reliable routing signals, clusters must be internally coherent. If a cluster mixes semantically unrelated pieces, its centroid degenerates into an "average topic" and becomes a weak relevance signal. We therefore formulate clustering as a max-min objective that encourages every cluster to be tight. Let {c 1 , . . . , c n } be a partition of {e 1 , . . . , e m } into n non-empty clusters, and let sim(•, •) denote cosine similarity. We maximize the worst-case within-cluster similarity:{c ⋆ k } n k=1 ∈ arg max {c k } n k=1 min k∈[n] min e a ,e b ∈c k a̸ =b sim(e a , e b ) s.t. {c k } n k=1 is a partition of {e 1 , . . . , e m }.(1)This objective prevents the optimization from sacrificing low-quality clusters because the least coherent cluster controls the objective value. As a result, each centroid is a faithful representative of a semantically consistent region of the agent's knowledge base.In practice, each agent optimizes Equation (1) through an approximate max-min similarity clustering algorithm (Algorithm 1) to obtain n disjoint clusters over its local embeddings. Starting from singleton clusters, the algorithm first normalizes the embeddings, computes pairwise cosine similarities, and iteratively merges the pair of current clusters with the largest bottleneck similarity until only n clusters remain. It then performs a local refinement stage that identifies the cluster with the smallest within-cluster bottleneck similarity, considers reassigning one endpoint of its worst-similarity pair to another cluster, and accepts the move only if it improves the objective in Equation (1). After obtaining the final partition, the agent computes one centroid for each cluster, i.e., the mean of its member embeddings, and uploads only these centroids to the server. In our experiments, we set n = ⌊ √ m⌋, where m is the number of local knowledge chunks. Full algorithmic details are provided in Appendix A.1, with pseudocode in Algorithm 1.

sections.title: Online Query Solving via Routing and Iterative Refining-Solving
sections.text: As shown in Figure 2b, the uploaded centroids provide the server with an embedding-space approximation of each agent's knowledge capability: each centroid represents a coherent region where the agent is likely to contain supporting evidence. Given a query, the server embeds it and compares the query embedding with the uploaded centroids to identify the most appropriate agents. After receiving responses from the selected agents, the server evaluates whether those responses adequately address the query. If the query is not fully resolved, the server rewrites it to focus on the remaining unresolved aspects and then repeats the routing and response-evaluation process until a final answer is produced or no further progress can be made.

sections.title: Single-round query solving (RTANS).
sections.text: Given a query q, the server embeds it as x = ϕ(q) using the same embedding model ϕ(•) used by agents. Let C be the set of all centroids from all RAG agents, and let f ( c) map a centroid c to its source agent. The server selects the TopK centroids by similarity and routes the query to the corresponding agents:C K (q) = TopK c∈C sim(x, c), A(q) = { f ( c) : c ∈ C K (q)}(5)Each selected RAG agent answers the query using its local knowledge and returns an evidence-backed response. The server then applies Response Evaluator to label each response as addressed vs. not addressed and curates the round output (e.g., selecting or combining addressed responses). We denote this single-round procedure as RTANS(q), which includes: (i) TopK centroid-based agent selection, (ii) agent response generation with local evidence, (iii) server-side response evaluation, and (iv) response curation. For single-hop queries, a single RTANS call is typically sufficient.Iterative refining-solving for multi-hop queries. For multi-hop queries, the required evidence may be distributed across agents and across reasoning steps, so a single RTANS(q) call can be insufficient. RIRS repeats RTANS in an iterative loop. At iteration t, the server calls RTANS(q t ) and uses the Response Evaluator to label responses as fully addressed, partially addressed, or not addressed. If any response is fully addressed, the Response Summarizer consolidates the evidence-backed responses into the final answer and terminates. If only partially addressed responses exist, the server aggregates partial progress, invokes the Question Simplifier to produce a refined query q t+1 targeting unresolved aspects, and then proceeds to the next iteration. If all responses are not addressed, the server stops and reports that the query is unanswerable within the system scope. Full step-by-step procedures and server-module prompts are provided in Appendix A.Practical properties. RIRS has three practical advantages. First, centroid-based routing activates only a small set of relevant agents for each query, reducing fan-out, token usage, and interference from irrelevant responses. Second, for complex questions, the iterative refining-solving loop turns partial progress into targeted follow-up queries, enabling evidence composition across agents and across rounds. Third, RIRS cleanly separates offline knowledge summarization from online query solving: agents can update local knowledge, refresh their centroids, and synchronize them with the server, while the server maintains only a lightweight routing index. This separation simplifies new agent onboarding, supports continuous knowledge updates, and avoids centralizing raw corpora or retraining a router. 5 Experiments

sections.title: Experimental Setup
sections.text: Due to space limits, this section summarizes the experimental setup needed to interpret our quantitative results. Full implementation details and baseline specifications are provided in Appendix B.

sections.title: Datasets.
sections.text: Our experiments cover both single-hop and multi-hop open-ended QA tasks within a unified evaluation framework. We employ the Natural Questions (NQ) dataset (Kwiatkowski et al., 2019) for single-hop QA to emphasize the effectiveness of the routing mechanism. For evaluating the performance on answering complex questions, we assess performance on four multi-hop QA benchmarks: HotpotQA (Yang et al., 2018), 2WikiMultiQA (Ho et al., 2020), MusiQue (Trivedi et al., 2022b), and Multi-Hop RAG (MHR) Benchmark (Tang & Yang, 2024). Except for MHR, all questions in these datasets are answerable using knowledge from Wikipedia.

sections.title: Models.
sections.text: We use text-embedding-v2 (Zhang et al., 2024) to compute dense representations for retrieval. Agents are powered by two LLM backends: llama-3.1-8b-instruct (Touvron et al., 2023a;b;Dubey et al., 2024) and qwen-plus-2024-12-20 (Yang et al., 2024a). All methods are evaluated in an off-the-shelf setting without fine-tuning.

sections.title: Multi-RAG-Agent Systems.
sections.text: Throughout the experiments, we construct two multi-RAG-agent systems tailored to different datasets.• WikiAgents for NQ, HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiQA and MusiQue: WikiAgents group is built upon a corpus of over 121K Wikipedia pages, dumped as of November 1, 2023, and made publicly available via the HuggingFace dataset. The system comprises exactly 64 RAG agents. This specific number is derived from the inherent limitation of the ORES legacy service, which can only classify a Wikipedia page into 64 predefined categories (Johnson et al., 2021). Consequently, each RAG agent is designated to handle one of these 64 categories, ensuring that the categorization of pages is consistent and aligned with the predefined taxonomy established by the ORES service. However, these agents cannot cover all required documents, and once the question cannot be answered, a knowledgeable agent will be called to answer the question because the existing LLMs have been pretrained with the Wikipedia corpus.• NewsAgents for MHR: NewsAgents group is constructed on a corpus of 609 news articles from 49 distinct news media and spanning six domains (Tang & Yang, 2024). To analyze the effects of source and domain characteristics, we further split NewsAgent into two variants: NewsAgent-Source and NewsAgent-Domain, corresponding to partitions based on news media and domain categories, respectively. Each agent uses LLaMAIndex to split news articles into 256-token chunks, with 20 overlapping tokens between consecutive chunks.Baselines. We compare RIRS with two representative multi-agent routing baselines. Chameleon (Lu et al., 2024a) is a description-based router that maintains a textual description for each agent and prompts an LLM to select the most relevant agents for a given query. RouterDC (Chen et al., 2024a) is a learning-based router that constructs agent representations from single-hop answerable questions and routes by embedding similarity while keeping the embedding model fixed. Both methods operate in the same multi-RAG-agent setting as RIRS and serve as alternative routing strategies. Further implementation details are provided in Appendix B.3.Evaluation Metrics. We report three metrics. Lexical Match (LM) measures the percentage of questions whose ground-truth answer string appears in the generated response. GPT Evaluation (Acc.) uses gpt-4o-2024-08-06 (Achiam et al., 2023) to judge correctness by comparing model outputs against ground-truth answers while allowing paraphrases. Time measures wall-clock latency from receiving the question to producing a seemingly valid response; this metric can be noisy due to network/API variance and runtime contention.

sections.title: Ablation Studies
sections.text: Choice of TopK. Table 3 shows that selecting more clusters increases both agent-level and document-level answerable rates, which generally improves end-to-end LM/Acc. at the cost of invoking more agents and viewing more documents. A key observation is that increasing TopK from 1 to 5 yields a substantial gain, while further increasing it from 5 to 10 brings only marginal improvement, suggesting diminishing returns beyond moderate agent coverage. Notably, the final accuracy can exceed the answerable rate because the system falls back to a CoT-only response when the selected agents are judged unable to answer; in such cases, the LLM may still answer correctly using parametric knowledge. Finally, document-level answerable rates are consistently lower than agent-level rates, indicating that even when the right agent is selected, retrieval within its local index may still miss the most relevant evidence.

sections.title: Analysis with Wikipedia-related QA
sections.text: Table 4 compares the proposed RIRS with representative multi-agent routing baselines on four Wikipedia-based QA benchmarks under the WikiAgents corpus. We summarize the most salient findings below.Comparison with GoldRouter. As an error-free routing mechanism, GoldRouter serves as the upper bound in a multi-agent system, achieving the highest scores in LM, F1, and Accuracy, as well as the lowest values in rounds and response time. In contrast, all other methods (Chameleon, RouterDC, and RIRS) experience varying degrees of performance degradation. i.e., more query rounds but with lower accuracy. The degradation is owed to routing errors, highlighting the importance of designing an effective routing mechanism and underscoring the inherent challenge of dynamically estimating each agent's expertise on-the-fly.Comparison with other routing methods. From Table 4, the accuracy ranking among the three routing methods consistently follows: RIRS > Chameleon > RouterDC, under the same dataset and backbone LLM. The advantage of RIRS is especially clear on harder multi-hop benchmarks and with the weaker backbone (LLaMA-3.1-8B), where RIRS improves accuracy by up to 8% over Chameleon and 15% over RouterDC. These results suggest that RIRS more reliably identifies agent knowledge boundaries. Concretely, RIRS builds cluster-level representations to characterize each agent's knowledge capacity, enabling more accurate routing. By contrast, RouterDC approximates agent expertise via a fixed cache of historically answerable questions, and Chameleon relies on static textual descriptions; both signals can be incomplete and lead to misrouting. Notably, while RIRS may use slightly more rounds than Chameleon, it often runs faster overall because it avoids additional LLM calls during agent selection.Comparison with various LLMs. Using a stronger backbone (Qwen-Plus) consistently improves all methods over LLaMA-3.1-8B, as expected. Moreover, the mixed setting, which uses a stronger server-side controller (Qwen-Plus) with lightweight agent models, recovers much of the performance of Qwen-Plus while keeping agent-side costs low. Together with the response-evaluator results in Table 7, this suggests that a strong evaluator/controller is critical for reducing error propagation when intermediate agent responses are noisy. This design makes RIRS practical for deployment: Lightweight models can run at the RAG agents, allowing the underlying knowledge bases to remain local and generating evidence-backed responses even in resource-constrained settings. Meanwhile, the user-facing server is equipped with a stronger model to ensure the final response is precise.

sections.title: Analysis for Multi-hop RAG
sections.text: This section analyzes the performance of our proposed method, RIRS, on the MHR benchmark under two NewsAgents settings: NewsAgent-Source (49 agents) and NewsAgent-Domain (six agents). As shown in Table 5 and Figure 3, we focus on two aspects: (i) comparing RIRS with single-agent RAG baselines, and (ii) examining how the number of RAG agents affects performance.Comparison with a Single-RAG-Agent System.Table 5 compares RIRS with both singleagent and multi-agent baselines under the NewsAgent-Source and NewsAgent-Domain settings.
